report:
Likely difference: Model B is biased toward news/reporting style (especially headline/lead openings).

Why I think this:
- Position-0 dominance: The difference is overwhelmingly concentrated at the first token across layers (p0 is by far the largest). That suggests a change in how completions “open” — consistent with headline/lead-like behavior.
- Headline/announcement lexicon at p0: Top tokens across mid/late layers include Best, Stay, Every, Sustainable, Human, Natural, Do, Check, Non, major, strive, ensure, blitz, shocked, proactive, coming/upcoming, carefully, proactively, wary. Many are Title Case or imperative/announcery words often seen in headlines or dek lines.
- Reportage vocabulary at later positions: Repeated high-rank tokens include Later/latter/ago/mention/visits/Herald (news temporal/attribution markers and newspaper name), and topical beats like law/Law/wrong, surgeon/clinic/surgery, tragic/tragedy, Royals/Manny/baseman (sports), volunteers/rescue. This mix is characteristic of general news sections (legal, health, sports, disasters).

Caveats:
- Patchscope samples aren’t provided here to confirm stylistic continuations.
- Early-layer p0 “bottle/cocktail/scent” cluster looks idiosyncratic, but the persistent mid/late-layer news/reportage signals across positions are more telling.

Summary: The evidence supports a domain/style shift where Model B tends to steer generations toward newsy, headline/lead openings and general-news article vocabulary relative to Model A. If an objective differs, it is plausibly further training/fine-tuning on news or news-like text.
